## IRA Account Types: An Overview
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/cash-stack.svg
For an individual earning $70,000 annually, understanding the differences between a Roth IRA and a Traditional IRA is crucial for optimizing tax benefits and planning for future withdrawals. The primary distinctions lie in when your money is taxed and the flexibility of accessing funds before retirement.

## Roth vs. Traditional IRA: A Detailed Comparison
Here's a breakdown of the key features of each IRA type, with a focus on tax implications and early withdrawal rules for an earner at your income level.

- **Contribution Limit (2024):** $7,000 (under age 50); $8,000 (age 50 and over)

| Feature | Roth IRA | Traditional IRA |
| :-------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Tax Deductibility (Contributions)** | Contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are **not tax-deductible**. | Contributions may be **tax-deductible**, reducing your current taxable income. For a single filer earning $70,000, contributions are generally fully deductible. |
| **Tax on Growth & Qualified Withdrawals** | Earnings grow **tax-free**. Qualified withdrawals in retirement (after age 59.5 and 5-year rule met) are **tax-free**. | Earnings grow **tax-deferred**. Withdrawals in retirement are taxed as **ordinary income**. |
| **Income Limits for Direct Contributions** | For 2024, direct contributions begin to phase out for single filers with Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) between $146,000 and $161,000. A $70,000 earner can contribute directly. | No income limit for contributions, but deductibility may phase out if you are covered by a workplace retirement plan. For a $70,000 earner, this is not an issue. |
| **Early Withdrawal of Contributions (before 59.5)** | Your original contributions can be withdrawn **tax-free and penalty-free** at any time. | Withdrawals are generally subject to **ordinary income tax and a 10% penalty**, unless an exception applies. |
| **Early Withdrawal of Earnings (before 59.5)** | Earnings withdrawals are subject to **ordinary income tax and a 10% penalty** if the account is less than 5 years old OR if you don't meet a qualified exception. | Earnings withdrawals are subject to **ordinary income tax and a 10% penalty**, unless an exception applies (e.g., first-time home purchase, qualified education expenses, unreimbursed medical expenses). |
| **Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs)** | No RMDs for the original owner during their lifetime. | RMDs generally begin at age 73 (or 75, depending on birth year). |

## Contextual Assumptions
- We assume the $70,000 annual income refers to your Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI).
- We assume you are a single tax filer for determining income thresholds.
- Contribution limits and income thresholds are based on 2024 IRS guidelines.
